question: Zoho technical interview (resume-focused round), operating systems questions: **Explain thrashing, paging and threading.** Other questions in the same round included renaming a file in Linux and writing a script to list filenames by wildcard patterns.
lookingFor: Accurate definitions with the relationship between paging and virtual memory.
Understanding why thrashing occurs and how to prevent it.
Clear distinction between threads and processes.
answer:
**Paging.** A memory-management scheme where a process's logical (virtual) address space is divided into fixed-size **pages** and physical memory into equal-sized **frames**. A **page table** maps each page to a frame, so a process need not occupy contiguous physical memory. This removes external fragmentation (internal fragmentation can remain in the last page). With **virtual memory** and demand paging, only the pages that are actually needed are kept in RAM; the rest stay on disk. Accessing a page that is not in memory causes a **page fault**, and the OS loads it, possibly evicting another page using a replacement policy such as LRU or FIFO. A **TLB** caches recent translations to speed lookups.

**Thrashing.** A state where the system spends most of its time swapping pages in and out instead of executing useful work. It happens when the combined working sets of active processes exceed the available RAM, so page-fault rates become very high; CPU utilisation drops, and a naive scheduler may then admit even more processes, making it worse.

*Remedies:* reduce the degree of multiprogramming (suspend or swap out processes), add more RAM, use the **working-set model** or page-fault-frequency control to give each process enough frames, and improve locality in programs. Local page replacement also limits one process from stealing others' frames.

**Threading.** A **thread** is the smallest unit of CPU execution within a process. Threads of one process share code, heap and open files, but each has its own stack, registers and program counter. Compared to processes, threads are cheaper to create and switch, and communicate easily through shared memory; the cost is the need for **synchronisation** (mutexes, semaphores) to avoid race conditions and deadlocks. Multithreading allows concurrency (and parallelism on multicore CPUs) for example a server handling many requests or a UI thread staying responsive while a worker thread loads data.

**Quick contrast:** paging is about how memory is organised, thrashing is a performance failure of paging, and threading is about how work is executed.
